title: Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries
desc: A study of longitudinal cohorts from Europe and the United States over 30 years showed that later-born generations benefit from higher cognitive capacity and memory stability, which may explain the trend of declining dementia incidence rates. The risk of developing dementia at any given age has fallen steadily in Europe and the United States over recent decades. A key unresolved question is whether recent generations reach older age with better cognitive capacity, experience slower cognitive decline, or both, as this has implications for when preventive interventions are likely to have the greatest impact. Analyzing ~783,000 episodic-memory assessments from ~219,000 individuals in five longitudinal studies followed for up to 30 years, we find that later-born generations benefit from a double dividend, with higher memory levels entering old age and slower decline thereafter. The combined advantage is large enough to plausibly account for the reported 13% per-decade decline in dementia incidence. Improvements are concentrated among the fastest decliners; later-born generations show longer periods of stable memory, and their slower decline is mirrored by lower rates of clinical impairment and slower hippocampal atrophy. Calendar-time trends affecting all generations simultaneously are unlikely to explain these differences. Because memory level is built mainly in early life whereas the rate of decline is shaped by conditions in adulthood, sustaining the decline in dementia incidence will require prevention policies that protect brain health across the whole lifespan, beginning in childhood.

title: FIRE-EVIDENCE: enabling LLM-driven, machine-readable evidence synthesis for women’s health
desc: Clinical evidence is abundant in the published literature yet remains fragmented and underutilized, particularly in women’s health and menopause, where timely, personalized decision-making is critical. Conventional evidence synthesis relies on resource-intensive manual review, limiting scalability and delaying translation into practice, while automated approaches often produce outputs that are not directly computable or integrable into decision-support workflows. We present FIRE-EVIDENCE, a large language model framework that transforms full-text clinical studies into structured, Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-aligned computable evidence. The pipeline was optimized on seven development documents and evaluated on two datasets: a primary dataset of 26 expert-annotated randomized controlled trials and a secondary dataset of 18 studies derived from five systematic reviews. Across expert-annotated trials, FIRE-EVIDENCE achieved 94.35% completeness, 94.61% correctness, 97.36% source faithfulness, and an F _1 score of 94.43%. FHIR-compliance testing in a 10-output native FHIR-R5 subset showed that all validated outputs passed base HL7 FHIR validation without errors. FIRE-EVIDENCE demonstrates a feasible pathway for standard-based, machine-readable evidence synthesis.

title: Multimodal LLM for Breast Cancer Radiotherapy Target Auto-Contouring and Planning
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Xiaohui Zhao; conditions: Breast Cancer, Radiotherapy; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 51000; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Breast cancer remains the most prevalent malignancy among women worldwide, with a continuously increasing incidence. As a crucial component of comprehensive cancer treatment, radiotherapy plays a key role in reducing local recurrence rates and improving overall survival outcomes. However, traditional radiotherapy target volume contouring and treatment planning design rely heavily on clinician expertise, presenting challenges such as prolonged processing time, significant inter-observer variability, and high subjectivity in dose optimization. Although artificial intelligence has made substantial progress in automated contouring and planning, conventional single-modal models still face major limitations. These models struggle to effectively integrate clinical text, tumor biological characteristics, and dose distribution factors, resulting in restricted generalizability. Therefore, developing an intelligent radiotherapy assistance system capable of multimodal data fusion is of high clinical significance to enhance precision and efficiency in breast cancer radiotherapy. This study aims to develop an innovative breast cancer radiotherapy assistance system based on a multimodal large language model. By integrating multimodal imaging data (including CT, MRI, and ultrasound), pathology reports, and structured electronic health record text, the system realizes end-to-end intelligence from target volume contouring to treatment plan generation. Employing a multicenter, ambidirectional cohort design, the study collects comprehensive clinical data from breast cancer patients who have undergone breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy. Technologically, the system innovatively combines the natural language processing capabilities of large language models with the image analysis strengths of deep learning, utilizing attention mechanisms to achieve deep fusion and interactive comprehension of heterogeneous medical data. Notably, the system breaks through traditional radiotherapy planning workflows by jointly optimizing target contouring and dose planning as a unified pipeline, applying reinforcement learning algorithms to dynamically balance target volume coverage with organ-at-risk protection. The outcomes of this study will provide an important paradigm for the clinical application of AI in radiation oncology and advance the field of precision radiotherapy.

title: Clinician Acceptance of Large Language Model-Generated Discharge Summaries.
desc: [JAMA network open] Hospital discharge summaries are essential for continuity of care, but fragmented electronic health record (EHR) data can compromise their quality and safety. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for clinical documentation tasks despite limited evidence regarding their performance in health care settings compared with the current standard of care. To evaluate clinician acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries derived from EHRs compared with routine clinician-written summaries. In this retrospective comparative effectiveness study using a prespecified noninferiority framework, acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries was compared with clinician-authored discharge summaries. Admission records from 5 London hospitals for September 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023, were evaluated against the full admission record by practicing physicians. Admissions were eligible only if the clinician-authored discharge summary contained identifiable clinical summary, plan and requested actions, and information given sections. Data analysis was conducted from July 2025 to February 2026. LLM-generated summaries were produced using GPT-4o mini (July 18, 2024 release; OpenAI) and a clinician-codesigned prompt. The primary outcome was clinician signoff with no or minor edits, derived from 2 sequential questions: (1) whether the reviewer would sign the summary and (2) whether no, minor, or major edits were required. A 5-percentage-point noninferiority margin was prespecified. Secondary outcomes assessed accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, poor; 2, fair; 3, good; 4, very good; and 5, excellent) and potential harmfulness of missing or incorrect information (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, no harm; 2, minor harm; 3, moderate harm; 4, high harm; and 5, extremely high harm). The study sample included 1294 (649 clinician-authored and 645 LLM-generated) unique case discharge summaries that were evaluated against the full admission record by 12 practicing physicians. title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
desc: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

title: Uncovering the Invisible in Routine Radiology: Cross-Modal Detection of MRI-Verified Soft-Tissue Pathologies from CBCT via Physics-Guided 3D Self-Supervised Learning
desc: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.

title: A Biologically Interpretable Single-Cell Pathology Foundation Model for Molecular Decoding of H&E Images
desc: The microscopic structure of human tissues encodes molecular information that is not directly accessible by visual inspection. Current pathology foundation models improve histological interpretation but operate at multicellular resolution. It remains unclear whether routine histology contains structured molecular and cellular information recoverable at single-cell resolution, which biological properties are associated with this recoverability, and where its limits lie. Here, we introduce Loki2, a single-cell pathology foundation model trained on UniSeg, a pan-tissue resource integrating 15 million cells with segmentation, lineage annotations and measured or histology-inferred transcriptomic profiles. We examine the above question across cellular representation, molecular recoverability, and patient-level relevance. Loki2 captures cellular identity and continuous morphological variation, with interpretable latent dimensions linked to physical nuclear phenotypes through DAPI validation. Transcriptomic retrieval and in silico protein staining test molecular recoverability, with gene-level analyses revealing the strongest recovery for genes associated with morphologically distinct cellular identities and functions. Then, patient staging and biomarker discovery connect cellular morphology representations to clinical relevance. Together, these findings establish Loki2 as a biologically interpretable single-cell pathology foundation model and provide the opportunities of recovering cellular and molecular information from routine H&E histology at single-cell resolution.

title: Human-Agentic AI Collaboration Workflow for Trend Analysis of ChatGPT Applications in Healthcare
desc: Background: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated strong potential to transform healthcare research and practice. However, LLMs are probabilistic and generate inherently variable outputs, which create risk and uncertainty in healthcare applications. Therefore, analyzing the current research landscape of ChatGPT applications is imperative to understand applied techniques and related concerns and to facilitate their practical integration into healthcare information systems. Objective: Leveraging LLM-based agentic AI with domain experts to analyze trends in ChatGPT healthcare applications and to examine the collaborative and interpretative capacities of LLM agents in broader contexts beyond narrowly defined topics. Methods: The review used a systematic search of the PubMed and Web of Science databases, following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and focused on ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors. To support the review process, an adaptive, iterative LLM-based agentic AI with a human-in-the-loop mechanism was employed for automated metadata extraction, identification, classification, and knowledge synthesis. The extracted information was subsequently used for temporal and thematic analyses, citation network construction, and main-path analysis. Results: Across 192 papers, the review identified 511 ChatGPT application types, 690 concern items, and 368 influence usage factors distinct from traditional IT, achieving a metadata error rate of 1.04%. The human-agentic AI workflow enabled efficient synthesis of contextual information across studies, addressing the growing challenge of timely evidence integration in medical knowledge. The findings provide insights into the evolving trajectories of ChatGPT applications in healthcare and demonstrate the value of an expert-validated human-agentic AI workflow in supporting literature analysis and streamlining review processes. Conclusion: This review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors in healthcare. The study further provides meaningful insights into the operational mechanisms of agentic AI, demonstrating the potential of human-AI collaboration for medical informatics research.

title: Routine laboratory trajectories predict organ-level complications in cancer
desc: Routine laboratory panels drawn during cancer treatment constitute longitudinal physiological recordings of organ function, yet their temporal structure is discarded by single-timepoint prognostic tools. A transformer trained on 2,777,595 laboratory measurements from 3905 patients with multiple myeloma or ovarian cancer predicted which of 162 treatment-associated complications would be newly recorded within two years, spanning eight clinical categories, achieving 1.5- to 6.1-fold enrichment above prevalence. Across individual endpoints it exceeded non-sequential baselines, including engineered-trajectory models, by +0.024 to +0.070 in mean AUROC. Predictions generalised across both cancers, divergence concentrating in disease-specific complications, and biomarker masking recovered signatures consistent with established pathophysiology. External validation on MIMIC-IV and MMRF CoMMpass showed transferability, strongest for renal and metabolic endpoints, attenuated for infection endpoints. On CoMMpass it added prognostic value to ISS staging. Routine oncological laboratory data carry complication-specific physiological signal months before a complication is recorded, and require no testing beyond standard oncological care.

During these procedures, surgeons operate while viewing images from laparoscopic endoscope. Key anatomical structures, such as the kidney, renal artery and vein, ureter, renal pelvis, inferior vena cava, and left reproductive vein, as well as surgical targets such as tumors, may sometimes be difficult to distinguish because of bleeding, surgical smoke, tissue movement, changes in tissue appearance, or obstruction by surgical instruments. The study team has developed an AI-based image recognition system that analyzes surgical video in real time and identifies and outlines relevant anatomical structures on the screen during surgery. The study has two main goals (primary endpoints): 1. To evaluate how accurately the AI system can identify and delineate key anatomical structures in surgical videos collected from different hospitals, surgeons, surgical procedures, and imaging systems. 2. title: The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Facial Plastic Surgery: From Education and Research to EHR-Embedded Applications.
desc: [Facial plastic surgery : FPS] Aims and Backgrounds Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly relevant to facial plastic surgery. This narrative review examines applications in education, research, and clinical workflows, including tools embedded in the electronic health record (EHR), and discusses responsible adoption. Technology Applications include educational content generation, surgical skill assessment, facial measurement, research assistance, preoperative simulation and planning, decision support, chart summarization, ambient documentation, and patient-message drafting. Agentic workflows could coordinate clinical tasks. Current and Future Development Available evidence primarily evaluates feasibility, content quality, measurement agreement, and workflow effects rather than improved clinical outcomes. Hallucinations, readability, privacy, safety, and bias require attention. Priorities include external validation, outcome assessment, and governance with continued monitoring as systems change. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance AI should augment surgeons, with oversight proportionate to clinical risk, protection of patient information, and assessment across patient groups. Its value should be judged by demonstrated improvements in clinical work, patient experience, and meaningful outcomes.

title: When Expert Disagreement Hurts: Prestige and Selectivity in LLM Decision Revision
desc: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers. We introduce a controlled two-pass audit that holds the question, the evidence, and the model's initial answer fixed and varies only the revision context: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a domain expert. For binary decisions the accounting is exact: revision raises accuracy only if it is selective enough, reversing wrong answers more than a/(1-a) times as often as correct ones, where a is initial accuracy (nine times at 90%). Across five models and 1,989 evidence-grounded decisions in medicine, science, and law, no model clears this bar under expert disagreement, and accuracy falls by up to 16.1 points. The expert label, a prestige cue, adds reversals for four of the five models, yet its effect on accuracy ranges from a 5.2-point loss to a 2.4-point gain, so reversal counts are a poor proxy for harm. With identical arguments from both sources, the label still raises reversal for three proprietary models and in a pooled analysis of four newer models. Models also respond to stated source reliability. Revision pipelines should therefore be evaluated with paired, conditional metrics, per model and protocol.

title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
desc: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

title: Automated segmentation of renal structures using brightfield images of unstained kidney biopsies
desc: The automated segmentation of unstained kidney brightfield microscopy images remains a significant challenge in medical imaging. In conventional histopathology, staining provides crucial structural and molecular contrast, allowing renal compartments and structures to be readily distinguished. The absence of staining markedly reduces this contrast, obscuring the fine architectural details that are essential for diagnosis. Addressing this gap would reduce reliance on staining protocols, reduce technical and interpretive variability, and preserve valuable tissue for downstream molecular or multi-omics analyses. Ultimately, automation of unstained image segmentation could enable faster, more objective tissue analysis while preserving samples for further molecular testing. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art segmentation methods applied to renal brightfield microscopy images. Current findings highlight a predominance of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based architectures for semantic segmentation approaches while recent trends point to the growing application of transformer-based and instance-segmentation strategies. However, the field is still hampered by the scarcity and poor annotation of publicly available renal datasets. Aiming to further contribute to the enhancement of the field, a dataset of 18 Whole Slide Images (WSIs) of unstained human kidney tissue is made publicly available. Additionally, in the dataset, we provide 543 annotated tiles extracted from the WSIs, facilitating further research into stain-independent segmentation approaches. As a third contribution, we present a preliminary case study, evaluating state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation architectures, including U-Net and Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our preliminary results indicate that deep learning models demonstrate promising segmentation performance in unstained kidney biopsies. In alignment with these findings, advanced customised loss functions and data augmentation were integrated into the supervised training of the promising U-Net, DeepLabv3+, and TransUNet models, achieving significant improvements compared to the baseline experiments. To exploit the abundance of unlabelled data, we further tested FixMatchSeg, a semi-supervised learning method; however, its segmentation performance remained slightly behind the supervised methods. title: Recording sampling rate as a negative-control exposure for detecting measurement-driven bias in heart-rate-variability-outcome associations: a quantitative bias analysis across ICU waveform databases
desc: Importance. Heart-rate variability (HRV) is studied extensively as a prognostic marker in critical illness, yet the electrocardiographic sampling rate at which HRV is computed systematically distorts the resulting values. Whether the associations between HRV and clinical outcomes reported in the literature are partly a consequence of this distortion has not been examined directly. Objective. To evaluate whether between-database differences in native ECG sampling rate can be used as a negative-control exposure to detect measurement-driven bias in HRV-outcome associations, and to quantify the sensitivity of a published association to an empirically measured distortion coefficient using quantitative bias analysis (QBA). Part II derives a bias-correction factor under a multiplicative measurement-error model and propagates the empirical confidence interval of the distortion coefficient as a sensitivity band. Part III applies the procedure to an observed HRV-mortality association from a single ICU waveform database, and examines the separate bias arising from threshold-based categorisation. title: "Pipe-Laying": A novel fusion of 3D MRI and health records for the early detection and diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease using deep learning.
desc: [PloS one] Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a prevalent form of dementia that impacts brain cells. Although its likelihood increases with age, there is no transitional period between its stages. In order to enhance diagnostic precision, physicians rely on clinical judgments derived from interpreting health data, considering demographics, clinical history, and laboratory results to detect AD at an early stage. While patient cognitive tests and demographic information are primarily presented in text, brain scan images are presented in graphic formats. Researchers typically use different classifiers for each data format and then merge the classifier outcomes to maximize classification accuracy and utilize all patient-related data for the final decision. However, this approach leads to low performance, diminishing predictive abilities and model effectiveness. We propose an innovative approach that combines diverse textual health records (HR) with three-dimensional structural magnetic resonance imaging (3D sMRI) to achieve a similar objective in computer-aided diagnosis, utilizing a novel deep learning technique. Health records, encompassing demographic features like age, gender, apolipoprotein gene, and mini-mental state examination score, are fused with 3D sMRI, enabling a graphic-based deep learning strategy for early AD detection. The fusion of data is accomplished by representing textual information as graphic pipes and integrating them into 3D sMRI, a method referred to as the "pipe-laying" method. This unified approach enables simultaneous processing of textual health records and 3D sMRI data within a single convolutional framework. Experimental results from over 4000 sMRI scans of 780 patients in the AD Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset demonstrate that the pipe-laying method enhances recognition accuracy rates for Early Mild Cognitive Impairment (EMCI) and Late Mild Cognitive Impairment (LMCI) patients, accurately classifying all AD patients. In a 4-class AD diagnosis scenario, encompassing AD, LMCI, EMCI, Cognitively Normal (CN) accuracy improved from 86.87% when only 3D images were used to 90.00% when 3D sMRI and patient health records were included. Thus, the positive impact of combining 3D sMRI with HR on 4-class AD diagnosis was established.

title: GlyphAtlas: Disentangling Stroke Detail from Layout for Scene Text Synthesis
desc: Scene text synthesis requires stroke-accurate characters rendered in a specified layout, as well as visual coherence with the surrounding scene. To achieve this, existing methods commonly pre-render the target text at its intended locations to form a glyph image that jointly specifies layout and glyph structure. However, this representation ties the resolution of each glyph to its target region, limiting fine-grained stroke guidance for small, densely packed, or structurally complex text. To tackle this, we propose GlyphAtlas, a scene text synthesis framework that retains the glyph image as a spatial anchor and supplies fine-grained stroke references through a dedicated glyph atlas. The atlas renders and encodes each character or word in a separate cell, decoupling reference resolution from target-region size. We further introduce atlas-anchored attention, which lets each text region retrieve stroke detail only from its corresponding atlas cells to refine the coarse glyph structure provided by the glyph image. This coarse-to-fine conditioning simplifies stroke rendering while preserving explicit layout correspondence. We optimize GlyphAtlas with a mask-weighted flow matching objective and a timestep-weighted text perceptual loss for writing accuracy and background consistency. Random resolution augmentation of atlas cells supports adjustable atlas budgets at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GlyphAtlas achieves stroke-accurate synthesis of small, dense, and structurally complex text, zero-shot transfer to languages unseen during task-specific training, and leading performance in scenes with many text regions. project page: https://fr0zencrane.github.io/project-glyphatlas/

title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
desc: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning $T_1$w, FLAIR and $T_2$w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer.

title: AlphaGenome 2 predicts regulatory activity and variant effects across cell states
desc: Most genetic variants associated with human traits and diseases lie in non-coding DNA, where they can alter gene regulation in specific cell types and states. Single-cell atlases chart these states across tissues and development, but rarely profile enough donors to associate variants with expression directly. Deep learning models could bridge this gap by predicting variant effects from DNA sequence, yet they poorly distinguish related cell states and require fine-tuning for new datasets. Here we present AlphaGenome 2 (AG2), which substantially advances cell-type-specific prediction of regulatory activity and variant effects for gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Trained on organism-wide human and mouse single-cell atlases and bulk functional genomics data, AG2 takes as input a 1-Mb DNA sequence and a condition specifying a target tissue, cell type, or cell state. Conditioning enables AG2 to impute unmeasured epigenomic tracks and predict multimodal variant effects across cell types. Inferring this condition directly from gene expression extends AG2 to unseen datasets and cell states without fine-tuning. AG2 outperforms fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1 and specialized models trained on target datasets, doubling recall of causal single-cell eQTLs at 90% precision. AG2 also achieves state-of-the-art enhancer-gene linking and can pinpoint causal variants at complex trait loci. Across hundreds of human cell types, we generated an atlas of enhancer-gene links and scores for 7 million common variants. As single-cell profiling expands across development, tissues, and disease cohorts, AG2 provides a blueprint for turning observational atlases into variant effect maps.

title: Eye-to-Eye: Gaze detection as a proxy for medical doctor behaviour during virtual and in-person appointments
desc: The gaze direction of the physician during consultations plays an important role in patient satisfaction, with several studies pointing to the positive correlation between the amount of time the physician spends looking at the patient and patient satisfaction. Additionally, the effects of the virtual consultation environment on the gaze behaviour of the doctor have yet to be studied. Therefore, this study aims to assess the impact of the virtual consultation environment by comparing the amount of total time the doctor spends looking at the patient between face-to-face and virtual consultations, as well as the average duration during the consultation and the gaze frequency. The study population consisted of 14 doctors divided between 4 medical specialties: Gynaecology/Obstetrics (4), Neurology (3), Endocrinology (3) and General and Familiar Medicine (4). A low-cost desktop that runs an appearance-based gaze estimation pipeline was implemented in the clinical setup. Each doctor recorded 20 face-to-face consultations and 20 virtual consultations, which were then processed by the pipeline to obtain the percentage of time the doctor spent looking at the patient during the consultation. Overall, we found that doctors look more at the patient in virtual consultations compared to face-to-face consultations, both in total time and average duration during the consultation. Within medical specialties, three out the four specialties involved presented clear tendencies to look more at the patient in virtual consultations when compared to face-to-face consultations.

desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Shandong Provincial Hospital; conditions: Heart Failure, Outcome Assessment (Health Care), Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Diffusion Tensor Imaging, Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM); type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 2000; status: RECRUITING] Heart failure is a common condition in which the heart cannot pump blood effectively. Heart failure can lead to changes in the heart's structure and function, called cardiac remodeling, and to different risks of hospitalization or death. The main goals are to better understand cardiac remodeling in different types of heart failure and to find out whether combining information from different tests can improve risk stratification. title: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Hepatology: Emerging Opportunities and Translational Challenges.
desc: [Journal of clinical gastroenterology] In December 2025, the Food and Drug Administration assessed and qualified the first artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tool for use in drug development trials; this AI system evaluates digital liver biopsies for steatohepatitis and fibrosis. However, AI is still being investigated before it can be applied directly to patient care in the field of Hepatology. Current patient-facing applications at most institutions are limited to assistive tools such as computer-aided polyp detection and large language model documentation tools that draft clinic notes and patient communications, although there exist radiographic and pathologic liver AI tools that could function at and may even exceed human capabilities. This review provides a broad introduction to AI and highlights clinical research that use AI to enhance the diagnosis, prognostication, and management of liver diseases. It will also discuss the challenges that will need to be overcome before AI can be adopted to clinical practice.

title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
desc: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.

title: statLens enables accurate and interpretable statistical intelligence
desc: Diverse existing approaches and analyses of large-scale biomedical omics datasets along with the complexity of the corresponding statistical analytical workflows pose challenges to the direct application of large language models (LLMs) to data analysis tasks. We present statLens, a model-agnostic AI-driven statistical intelligence framework that integrates LLMs, code and human review. We demonstrate statLens using differential expression analysis across heterogeneous biomedical data as a use case. On 102 benchmark tasks from 74 datasets across six omics modalities, statLens maintained consistently high accuracy (92.5--95.0%) across seven language models and outperformed LLM-only inference (17.5--46.8%), whereas autonomous-agent accuracy varied widely (58.7--99.5%). We also showed that statLens substantially improved the accuracy of the four small language models (92.5--94.4%) over autonomous agents (58.7--92.2%) and LLM-only inference (17.5--43.5%). By decomposing analytical workflows into complementary tasks for code, LLMs and human experts, statLens provides an integrated framework for more accurate, interpretable and reproducible AI-assisted data analysis, particularly in complex omics settings.

title: Requirements of a knowledge support tool for self-harm in general practice: a mixed-methods study with patients, carers, and clinicians
desc: Background General practice has a central role in care following self-harm. However, clinicians frequently report uncertainty about best practice and patients describe poor care. A knowledge support tool is an add-on to electronic health systems that may improve services by providing personalised care information. Aim To understand what general practice clinicians, patients and carers need from a novel knowledge support tool for self-harm. Design and Setting Mixed-methods, using quantitative ratings, focus groups and follow-on interviews with general practice clinicians and patients/carers with lived experience of self-harm. Method Clinicians were recruited through social media and professional networks, and patients/carers through a third-sector organisation. During four focus groups and follow-on interviews, we explored the utility of potential content and functionality of a knowledge support tool. Quantitative utility ratings were summarised descriptively and qualitative data were analysed thematically using the framework method. People with lived/living experience were involved throughout. Results 13 clinicians and 14 patients/carers participated. Requirements of the knowledge support tool were captured across three qualitative themes: facilitating person-centred care, accessibility and usability, and balancing competing priorities of general practice. Across these themes, patients' and carers' needs were centred on promoting compassionate relationships and patient agency. Clinicians shared these needs but balanced them with a need to manage patient expectations and practice defensively under limited resources. Conclusion Our findings inform the core design of a knowledge support tool and suggest that such a tool could support the assessment and management of self-harm in general practice.

title: Beyond scales: Artificial intelligence, language, and behavior in suicide risk modeling-a narrative review.
source: PubMed · European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology
desc: [European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology] Suicide is a leading, preventable cause of premature mortality, yet identifying individuals at imminent risk remains difficult. There are no validated biomarkers for routine stratification, and common approaches (clinical interviews, rating scales, self-report) are limited by subjectivity, reporting bias, and weak positive predictive value for rare outcomes. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI)-including machine learning, deep learning, and large language models-offer opportunities to integrate heterogeneous signals relevant to risk and treatment response. This narrative review summarizes recent AI-enabled prediction and characterization of suicidal thoughts and behaviors across major data modalities: structured electronic health records and claims; natural language processing of clinical notes and digital text; speech and facial/behavioral signals; neuroimaging and other neurobiological measures; and passive sensing from smartphones and wearables. We review common modeling and evaluation practices, emphasizing clinically relevant performance assessment (discrimination and calibration) and the importance of temporal and external validation. We also highlight barriers to translation, including class imbalance and label noise, dataset shift across sites and time, limited prospective evaluation, and the need for interpretable outputs that can support medication decisions and care pathways (e.g., triage, monitoring, and stepped interventions). Ethical and implementation challenges-privacy and consent, algorithmic bias and equity, governance, and the clinical consequences of false-positive and false-negative predictions-are discussed with an emphasis on safe deployment. We conclude with priorities for the field, including multimodal longitudinal cohorts, harmonized reporting standards, and pragmatic trials to determine whether AI decision support measurably improves suicide-prevention outcomes.

title: OICycle: Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle for Belief-State Learning in Longitudinal Clinical Decision Making
desc: Clinical care is a closed loop: clinicians observe partial evidence, infer the patient's state, and intervene, and each intervention determines what is observed next. This makes clinical decision making a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which a belief over a latent patient state must be updated from irregular, multimodal, and incomplete records. Yet most deep clinical models predict from a single snapshot or from coarsely aggregated history, while POMDP-based clinical methods need hand-specified discrete state spaces and transition models that real electronic health records cannot supply. We introduce OICycle (Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle), which learns a stochastic belief state directly from retrospective trajectories. At every episode, a learned recurrent operator fuses a sample of the previous belief with the new multimodal observations and the intervention that produced them. The resulting Gaussian belief is trained to predict clinicians' next interventions, the time to the next episode, and next-episode mortality. To enable reproducible evaluation, we release a benchmark derived from MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-Note, and MIMIC-CXR that organizes 72,075 hospital admissions (5.4M laboratory, microbiology, radiology, prescription, and note records) into temporally ordered therapeutic--diagnostic episodes. Compared with an otherwise identical history-free model, OICycle improves next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347, time-to-next-episode macro-F1 from 0.293 to 0.351, and next-episode mortality macro-F1 from 0.585 to 0.649. Analysis shows that the learned belief encodes intervention type and trajectory position and evolves smoothly across episodes, and that the benefit of history is concentrated in interventions whose ordering depends on prior findings.

title: Savant: A Fast, Structure-Free Binding Affinity Predictor For Protein-Ligand Drug Screening
desc: Protein-ligand binding affinity determines which of many candidate molecules is worth synthesizing and assaying, making it the central measurement in early drug discovery. Binding affinity is commonly expressed as the dissociation constant, an equilibrium measure that indicates how easily a complex separates into its components. AI-based generative chemistry and make-on-demand chemical catalogs now produce molecules faster than rigorous method can evaluate them. Leading computational methods co-fold the complex before scoring the binding affinity between the protein and the ligand, which provides high accuracy but requires a graphics processing unit (GPU) and substantial time for every pair evaluated.Here we present Savant, a machine learning model that estimates the dissociation constant using only the protein's amino acid sequence and the ligand's structure written as a line of text (SMILES). Savant needs no 3-dimensional folded structure, no docking, and no GPU. To test Savant fairly, we built a benchmark designed to prevent any training data to leak into the testing set, drawing only on measurements published after the training data was assembled and on molecules chemically unlike anything the model had seen. On an independent benchmark, Savant ranks ahead of every other 3-dimensional structure-free method.Savant is designed to rank compounds against a single protein, and performs as well as other methods that require a GPU, while running only on a central processing unit (CPU). Thus, Savant can screen libraries of 100,000 compounds in minutes with commodity hardware.

title: Evaluation of System One Models on Biomedical Texts
desc: Objective To compare the performance and cost of System One models (SOMs) with general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on biomedical tasks and evaluate confidence-based routing. Materials and Methods We evaluated three SOMs and three LLMs across seven datasets and eight endpoints covering question answering, error detection, structured extraction, and clinical-note assessment. Outcomes included task-specific performance, recorded inference cost and latency, and confidence calibration. Calibration data determined routing schemes and confidence thresholds to evaluate test predictions, with cost-matched random referral as a comparator. Results Claude Opus 5.5 had the highest primary performance on all eight endpoints. The strongest SOM, Jev, had competitive performance with the evaluated LLMs and cost less than 1% of Opus on most datasets. Three selected SOM-to-LLM routes reduced costs by 30.0%-71.7% relative to the receiving LLM, with modest reductions in performance. On one benchmark, SOM-to-SOM routing achieved 91.1% accuracy, compared with 82.3% and 82.2% for the individual models. Discussion SOMs offered favorable performance-cost tradeoffs for most tasks. The magnitude of the advantages depended on task structure and prompting requirements. Confidence-based routing between SOMs and LLMs can leverage complementary model strengths and offers additional flexibility in performance-cost tradeoffs. The price advantages offered by SOMs can facilitate experimentation and development of workflows. This warrants further evaluation on closed datasets. Conclusion For biomedical tasks with predefined choices, SOMs represent a competitive stand-alone or first-stage approach.

title: Generating Medical Discharge Report Drafts Via Artificial Intelligence
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Kepler University Hospital; conditions: Patient Safety; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 40000; status: RECRUITING] A key process in intensive care is the creation of transfer reports. These summarize the essential aspects of the treatment to date and ensure that information is passed on to the next treatment team in a structured manner. The aim of a transfer report is to document the patient's medical history and the course of treatment to date in a concise and complete manner. Incomplete transfer reports can lead to repeated examinations, which can potentially delay further therapy and endanger the patient, as well as incurring additional costs. In this context, a complete transfer report ensures continuity of treatment and contributes significantly to patient safety. title: Artificial intelligence in radiology education: from AI-supported learning to clinical innovation-a narrative review.
desc: [Frontiers in medicine] Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing diagnostic radiology, but education and training have not kept pace. This narrative review brings together current evidence on AI-supported learning in radiology education and how such learning can move into clinical innovation. Surveys from different countries point to the same gap: in a 25-country international survey of radiographers, radiologists, and students, only 10.3% had received formal AI training; in one national survey of Turkish residents, 84.5% had received none. The review maps competency frameworks and curriculum models that define AI literacy and support staged integration into residency. It also assesses AI as a teaching tool, including AI-assisted case-based learning, computer-aided diagnosis training, precision-education knowledge recommenders, and virtual, augmented, and extended reality. Controlled and randomized studies show measurable gains: computer-aided diagnosis training raised resident scores above self-study controls (mean score 52 vs. 38 on a 100-point scale), while an AI-based knowledge recommender shortened reporting time by 162 s per case and relative improvement in graded reporting accuracy scores of 14% (95% CI 8.1-19.8%). Large language models are promising but limited: GPT-4 approaches board-style examination performance (80.6%) yet remains poor at image-based reasoning (47.8%). The review closes by considering how education can feed clinical innovation, along with algorithmic and automation bias, ethical governance, and future research needs. AI education should therefore span the full continuum-from undergraduate training to continuing professional development-if radiology is to innovate safely, effectively, and equitably.

title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine
desc: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Missense Variant Pathogenicity Prediction in the KCNQ Gene Family
desc: Missense variants in the KCNQ family of voltage-gated potassium channel genes are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological and cardiac disorders for which computational tools capable of differentiating benign and pathogenic variants are essential. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the first application of quantum machine learning (QML) to missense pathogenicity prediction. We employ a hybrid quantum framework combining data re-uploading quantum neural networks with quantum support vector machines and applied it to pathogenicity classification across the full KCNQ gene family. Systematic exploration of circuit architectures revealed that optimal hyperparameter choices enable the proposed quantum model to achieve predictive performance superior to or comparable to state-of-the-art classical machine learning approaches, reaching AUC-ROC values of approximately 0.94 across the full dataset. Although no clear quantum advantage is observed at present, these results demonstrate that quantum feature representations can effectively capture biologically relevant patterns in variant data and establish QML as a viable framework for future applications in computational genomics and precision medicine.

title: Microcirculation Mirror: A zero-install browser workstation for hand microvascular anatomy and nailfold capillaroscopy
desc: Background Hand microvasculature is conventionally presented through diagrams, cadaveric atlases and specialized optical instruments, while conventional clinical radiography cannot resolve individual capillary loops (5-15 m lumen) in vivo, which dominate cutaneous oxygen exchange. Methods We present Microcirculation Mirror, a zero-install browser workstation that registers layered hand anatomy to a live 21-landmark pose and couples it to a nailfold video capillaroscopy (NVC) simulator, a lumped microcirculatory model and an imaging-physics module. The single-file application runs offline on a laptop or, over local HTTPS, on a phone as an installable app. Results Its 3D atlas contains 136 named structures per hand in six systems from open Z-Anatomy/BodyParts3D meshes, plus a literature-parameterized capillary layer. The NVC module renders a 200x, 1.2-mm field with six deterministic patterns and quantified density, giant capillaries, avascular width fraction, hemorrhages, tortuosity and ramification. A lumped model reports nine estimates (SIM); a physics module shows that a 10-m capillary occupies 0.07 of a 150-m detector pixel; with iodinated contrast it retains {approx}0.016% effective contrast, about 60x below a 1% detection threshold; unenhanced blood is {approx}270x lower. The 2D stage renders in 2.9 ms per frame; system merging reduces atlas draw calls from 136 to 6. Conclusions The camera-overlay layers are templates, the atlas macro-anatomy is open mesh data, and the capillary layer is sampled. No patient data are used. The instrument is a product prototype, not a medical device, and provides a reproducible framework for making multi-scale microvascular reasoning visible.

title: AI Voice Calls Versus Text and Email Reminders for Questionnaire Response After Shoulder Arthroplasty
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Institut de Chirurgie Reparatrice Locomoteur et Sports; conditions: Shoulder Arthroplasty, Patient Reported Outcome Measures, Shoulder Pain; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 846; status: RECRUITING] After shoulder replacement surgery, surgeons send questionnaires to their patients to learn how they are doing (pain, shoulder function, satisfaction). Many patients do not answer. This study tests the best way to obtain these answers. The study is nested in a multicenter study of pain after shoulder arthroplasty conducted in four French centers (host study RetroPAinRSACAll, supported by Ramsay Santé). The clinical results of the host study are not the subject of this registration: this study evaluates only the method used to collect the information. All patients first receive an email invitation (when an email address is available) and, the next day, a text message (SMS) with a personal link to the questionnaire and a phone number to answer at any time by talking with an automated voice assistant. Patients who have not answered two days after the first contact are randomly assigned to one of two follow-up strategies: (1) further digital reminders (SMS on day 3 and day 5, email on day 7), or (2) up to three phone calls from a conversational artificial intelligence (AI) voice agent on days 3, 5 and 7, which asks the same questions orally. In both groups, patients can answer at any time online or by calling the voice assistant, and contacts stop as soon as the questionnaire is completed or the patient refuses. The main outcome is the proportion of patients who complete the questionnaire within 14 days of the first contact.

title: Using a Large Language Model Chatbot for Allergen Avoidance Counseling in Contact Dermatitis: Quantitative Evaluation Study.
desc: [JMIR dermatology] AI is increasingly impacting health care. Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have shown potential in supporting clinical decision-making. However, their application in dermatology, particularly in allergen avoidance counseling for contact dermatitis, remains underexplored. This study aimed to demonstrate a potential use case for LLM responses in recommending allergen-free products for the management of contact allergies. A total of 30 allergen groups included in the international standard patch test were assessed. ChatGPT (GPT-4) was used in this study from September 2023 to January 2024. For each allergen, ChatGPT was tasked with recommending 5 allergen-free products using 3 question formats of varying complexity. Responses were included if they specified a product and were manually classified by dermatologists into 5 categories: valid, invalid, cross-reaction, unknown, and unresponsive. ChatGPT provided 79.20% (1782/2250) valid responses, with 1.78% (40/2250) classified as invalid, 2% (45/2550) classified as cross-reactions, 8.67% (195/2250) classified as unknown, and 8.36% (188/2250) classified as unresponsive. The simplest question format yielded the highest proportion of valid recommendations (640/750, 85.33%). ChatGPT performed best when recommending cosmetics (1233/1365, 90.33%) and medications (198/240, 82.5%). However, lower validity rates were observed for recommendations involving certain sensitive allergens, including fragrance mixes and para-phenylenediamine (PPD), with frequent cross-reactive recommendations related to Peru balsam. The version of ChatGPT evaluated in this study showed potential as a supplementary tool for allergen avoidance counseling. However, its recommendations require verification and should not replace clinician guidance or established allergen avoidance resources.

title: PlainPairs: A Corpus Pairing the Prescriber and Patient Texts of U.S. Prescription Medicine Labels
desc: A prescription medicine in the United States comes with labeling written for prescribers, and many medicines also carry a text written for patients: a Medication Guide or a patient package insert. The two texts describe the same medicine for two readers, yet public resources rarely hold them side by side. I present PlainPairs, an open corpus built from the openFDA drug label files. Version 0.1.0 holds 35,177 prescription labels that carry a patient text, 21,416 distinct patient texts, 250,829 patient-text segments matched to prescriber sections through their regulatory headings, reading-level measures on both sides, and rule-based counts of plain-language wording. A second source, the National Cancer Institute's cancer information summaries, adds 756 summaries in health-professional and patient versions, in English and Spanish. Measured on the structure of the label, the median Medication Guide reads at grade 8.7 by Flesch-Kincaid and at grade 11.1 by SMOG. The same guides measured on the flattened text that the bulk files serve read about two grades higher, a difference that comes from lost list and heading boundaries. Patient texts address the reader in 41 of every 100 sentences, against 0.2 in prescriber sections. A blind hand check of 100 pairs supports the heading-based alignment for seven of ten heading types. The corpus, its code and its documents are public, and the release keeps texts that show a company copyright mark out of the text tables.

title: Deciphering the Biological Function of Tandem Mass Spectra Using a Dual-Modal Metabolite Language Model
desc: Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry untargeted metabolomics captures thousands of metabolic peaks from biological samples. Conventional identification-dependent metabolomics workflows require confident structural annotation before identified features can enter downstream pathway or functional analysis. However, only a small fraction of detected metabolic features can be assigned confident structural annotations, leaving a large fraction difficult to incorporate into downstream biological interpretation, a form of "functional dark matter". Here, we introduce Spec2Function, a function-centric framework that infers biological functions from tandem mass spectrometry (MS2) spectra. Spec2Function is trained using characterized spectrum-text pairs but does not require prior structural identification of the query spectra at inference time. At its core is Spec2Biotext, a dual-encoder contrastive model that embeds MS2 spectra and curated multi-aspect natural language functional texts into a unified functional space. Combined with a retrieval-augmented generation framework grounded in curated databases and biomedical literature, Spec2Function retrieves evidence-grounded biological knowledge and produces coherent functional summaries for individual spectra or groups of spectra. Across metabolite- and pathway-level benchmarks, Spec2Function achieved higher similarity to reference functional descriptions than the evaluated comparators and expanded the fraction of the metabolome accessible to functional interpretation. Application to a human liver cirrhosis cohort recapitulated known metabolic alterations and identified additional literature-supported functional modules. Applying Spec2Function to a 30-organ macaque aging atlas revealed organ-specific metabolic functions and previously unreported functional modules that were supported by independent human and mouse datasets. Together, these results position Spec2Function as a function-centric framework for scalable biological interpretation of structurally unannotated MS2 spectra.

title: Uncertainty-aware longitudinal prediction of multiple adverse pregnancy outcomes
desc: Risk of pregnancy complications is reassessed at each antenatal visit, but whether earlier predictions add information beyond the most recent one is unclear. Classifying every prediction as low or high risk can leave uncertainty unexpressed. Whether reliability per visit holds across visits is also unclear. This secondary analysis included 9289 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort (eight US centres, 2010-2013). Logistic regression models predicted gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, suspected fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age at 6-13, 16-21 and 22-29 weeks (Visits 3). Mondrian conformal prediction reported 'no' (low risk), 'yes' (high risk), or both (review). To test whether prediction history adds information beyond the Visit 3 prediction, we compared, among women classified as high risk at Visit 3, those first classified as high risk at Visit 2 or 3 (emerging high) with those classified as high risk at all three visits (persistent high), adjusting for Visit 3 predicted probability. The adjusted proportion with the outcome was higher in the emerging-high than the persistent-high group, by 6.1 percentage points for large for gestational age (95% CI -0.4 to 12.2) and 3.8 percentage points for suspected fetal growth restriction (-0.9 to 8.1). Other outcomes showed adjusted differences close to zero. With conformal prediction calibrated to a 90% level at each visit, the reported answers included the actual outcome in 89.6-90.6% of women at each visit (coverage). Coverage decreased when each woman's three visits were considered together (79.0-85.4%). For fetal growth outcomes, how a woman's predicted risk evolved during pregnancy may add information beyond her Visit 3 prediction. For repeated clinical use, the target coverage level should reflect the acceptable risk of incorrect low- or high-risk classifications over a woman's follow-up and the clinical decisions supported at each visit.

title: Assessment of AI-Assisted Ultrasound in DDH
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: The Hospital for Sick Children; conditions: Developmental Dysplasia of Hip, DDH, Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip, Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH), Hip Dysplasia; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 88; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is a condition in which a baby's hip joint does not develop normally. Ultrasound is commonly used to assess the hips of young infants for DDH, but these examinations usually require trained ultrasound staff and specialist interpretation. The purpose of this study is to determine whether a handheld ultrasound device combined with artificial intelligence (AI) can be used by non-specialist health care personnel to obtain and assess ultrasound images of infant hips. Infants attending the Baby Hip Clinic at The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) will undergo their usual clinical ultrasound as part of their standard care. They will also have an additional research ultrasound performed using the handheld device. Researchers will compare the research ultrasound with the standard clinical ultrasound. The study will assess the quality of the images obtained using the handheld device and compare the AI-assisted assessment with the diagnosis from the standard ultrasound and assessments made by experienced reviewers. The research ultrasound and AI results will not be used to make treatment decisions for participating infants.

title: Risks and Ethical Concerns of Artificial Intelligence in Plastic Surgery.
desc: [Clinics in plastic surgery] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping patient assessment, communication, and clinical decision-making in plastic surgery. Its potential benefits are accompanied by risks of plausible but inaccurate outputs, demographic and esthetic bias, compromised image privacy, and weakened human oversight. These risks become more consequential as systems move from providing information to recommending and executing clinical actions. This review examines the implications for patient safety, informed consent, equity, and professional accountability and outlines safeguards that scale with clinical risk and autonomy, emphasizing validation, continuous monitoring, and preservation of independent surgical judgment.

title: PeriaTrace: Tooth-Level Grounding Diagnosis and Patient-Facing Explanations from Periapical Radiographs
desc: Periapical radiographs (PRs) are central to endodontic diagnosis, but interpreting them and preparing reports are time-consuming. Technical language can limit patients' understanding, while existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. We present PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework integrating tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations and care recommendations. PeriaTrace was developed and evaluated using 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. In internal evaluation, it achieved a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35%, BLEU-4 of 0.6504, an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and a grounding-tag F1 score of 77.93%. In the two external cohorts, senior endodontists considered 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per PR, several tens of times faster than manual drafting. Among 196 survey participants without medical backgrounds, 96.4% preferred reports with plain-language explanations and care recommendations, and 84.7% found visual localization cues helpful. PeriaTrace may enable faster, evidence-traceable reporting while supporting clinical review and patient communication. (Abridged version)

title: S-PLM-TM enables fast and accurate sequence-based search for remote homologs
desc: Protein structures and functions can remain conserved after extensive sequence divergence, but detecting these distant relationships across large databases remains challenging. Here we present S-PLM-TM, a sequence-only remote homology search tool based on a structure-aware protein language model. Cross-modal flow matching and contrastive learning incorporate structural information into sequence representations. A lightweight calibration head enables structural-similarity search with the frozen encoder, while a residue-level alignment head generates structural alignments directly from sequence. S-PLM-TM outperforms the tested sequence-based methods in remote homology detection, rivals structure-based methods in structural classification and retrieves the most functionally consistent neighbors. It also retrieves distantly related enzymes with shared catalytic functions at a level comparable to the best-performing structure-based methods. In large-scale database search, S-PLM-TM achieves the highest average precision among both sequence-based and alignment-free methods, with speed approaching the fastest sequence-alignment tools. Together, these results establish S-PLM-TM as a practical tool that combines sensitive and biologically informative remote homology search with the speed required for database-scale retrieval.

Each patient is examined twice: first by a nurse using a handheld ultrasound probe with AI guidance, then by a radiologist as reference standard. The study measures image quality, agreement on free fluid between the nurse and the reference standard, and examination duration.

title: Deep learning denoising and deep learning-augmented contrast enhancement improve ultra-high-resolution photon-counting-detector CCTA image quality.
desc: [European radiology experimental] Ultrahigh-resolution (UHR) coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) using a photon-counting detector (PCD) provides excellent spatial resolution but is limited by increased image noise. We evaluated whether deep learning (DL)-based denoising and contrast enhancement can further improve UHR-CCTA image quality. UHR-CCTA scans from 25 patients with coronary artery disease were retrospectively analyzed. Images were reconstructed at 0.2-mm slice thickness without and with quantum iterative reconstruction (QIR, Qoff-Q4), and subsequently processed using a DL tool for denoising and increasing iodine contrast enhancement. Subjective image quality (sharpness, noise, vessel wall delineation, and overall quality) was assessed by three radiologists using a 5-point Likert scale. Objective analysis included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and coronary wall sharpness. Differences between image sets were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. DL-based CCTA demonstrated significantly superior subjective image quality across all parameters compared to standard reconstructions, with an overall median image quality ([interquartile interval, IQR]: 4 [3-5] versus 2 [2-3], p < 0.001). SNR and CNR were significantly higher for DL-based CCTA across all QIR levels (all p < 0.001). The highest values were observed for DL-based CCTAQ4 versus UHR-CCTAQ4 (SNR: 258.0 ± 147.5 versus 145.2 ± 50.1; CNR: 25.8 ± 17.1 versus 11.1 ± 4.5; both p < 0.001). Coronary wall sharpness was improved for DL-based CCTA for Q1-4 (all p < 0.027). DL-based denoising and iodine contrast enhancement effectively reduce noise and improve anatomic detail in UHR-CCTA, providing incremental value beyond vendor-specific reconstruction, particularly at high QIR strength levels. Question Deep learning reduces noise and enhances contrast in ultrahigh-resolution coronary CT angiography. Findings Image quality improves beyond standard iterative reconstruction methods, and vessel wall sharpness and diagnostic clarity significantly increase. Relevance statement This study aimed to determine at which levels of vendor-specific iterative reconstruction, DL-based denoising and contrast enhancement perform best in UHR CCTA, providing a foundation for future investigations on how these technical improvements may translate into diagnostic benefits.

title: VITAL: A Framework for Validating Agentic AI in Pharmaceutical Drug Development and Clinical Trial Operations
desc: Current assurance approaches do not establish whether evidence is sufficient to validate, monitor and govern agentic artificial intelligence (AI) within a pharmaceutical context of use. Plausible outputs may conceal failures in retrieval, reasoning, orchestration or human-control points, where reference standards are unavailable. We developed and operationalised VITAL (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence), a validation framework for agents in clinical development, through landscape analysis, regulatory and standards mapping, expert interviews and multi-stakeholder refinement. VITAL integrates context of use, controls, behavioural validation and lifecycle evidence within a risk-adjusted framework. We applied VITAL across epidemiology and treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrolment rescue and trial-design trade-off support to translate autonomy, reversibility, transparency and patient impact into proportionate validation activities, evidence requirements and auditable reconstruction of system behaviour. VITAL may inform evidence requirements and lifecycle accountability for higher-risk pharmaceutical uses; evaluation should assess reproducibility across assessors, organisations and system configurations.

title: Segment Anything for Microscopy 2
desc: Foundation models have advanced microscopy image segmentation, but existing models are trained on two-dimensional data, struggle with complex structures in volumetric data, and address only a narrow range of analysis tasks. Here we present Segment Anything for Microscopy 2 (SAM2), a foundation model that adapts SAM2 to joint 2D and 3D segmentation in light and electron microscopy. Trained on annotations of more than 23 million cells and nuclei and 1.6 million cellular structures, SAM2 achieves state-of-the-art automatic and interactive segmentation and outperforms generalist and specialist methods on volumetric data. Dedicated models further enable accurate mitochondrion and nucleus segmentation in electron microscopy. Beyond segmentation, SAM2 supports pixel and object classification from few annotations as well as cell tracking in 2D and 3D time-lapse data. All functionality is available in the user-friendly SAM napari plugin. We demonstrated the capabilities of SAM2 on challenging use cases spanning developmental biology, organoid research, cardiac physiology, and histopathology.
